text: Domain: number theory; integers n > 1. Units: none. The argument is invalid. Its premise—that n is divisible by 1 and by itself—is true for every integer n > 1, but this is only a necessary condition for primality, not a sufficient one. Primality requires that the only positive divisors of n are 1 and n (equivalently, that n has exactly two distinct positive divisors). Counterexample: n = 4. It is greater than 1 and divisible by 1 and 4, but it is also divisible by 2 (4 = 2 x 2), so 4 is composite, not prime. Corrected criterion: an integer n > 1 is prime if and only if its only positive divisors are 1 and n; equivalently, there is no integer d with 1 < d < n that divides n.
